newsitem.title: CROATIA: UN, Croatia to cooperate on two-way refugee return.
newsitem.headline: UN, Croatia to cooperate on two-way refugee return.

text.p: Croatia and the United Nations agreed on Friday to cooperate in returning both Croat and minority Serb refugees to their original homes in the country after the end of ethnic war.
Up to 150,000 displaced people inside Croatia, a little over half of them Croats, want to return home but face obstacles including a lack of housing and local ethnic hostility.
Senior U.N. and Croatian officials said after a meeting involving President Franjo Tudjman they had agreed to set up a working group to plan an orderly "two-way" return of displaced people.

This would mean Croats repopulating the now-Serb enclave of Eastern Slavonia, under U.N. administration but due to be reintegrated with the rest of the country this spring, and Serbs to former rebel areas which they fled when government troops recaptured them in 1995.

About 80,000 Croats want to resettle in Eastern Slavonia, a Croat majority region before it was seized by Serb separatists in 1991, and as many as 60,000 refugee Serbs now there may want to move back to old homes in western Croatia.
"We all agreed that a working group should be established to work out this two-way return," Sadako Ogata, the U.N. High Commmissioner for Refugees, told reporters after the meeting.
"(We want to) ensure the plan will be implemented in a way that will ensure equal access of (Serb and Croat) people to housing, economic reconstruction, pensions and various compensation mechanisms."
The working group will include representatives of the U.N. Transitional Authority in Eastern Slavonia (UNTAES).

Ivica Kostovic, Croatia's minister in charge of Eastern Slavonia issues, said: "We have agreed that the gradual, safe return of all the refugees is the key factor in the future process of peaceful reintegration."
One big problem will be finding housing for tens of thousands of refugee Serbs who now occupy homes which stand to be reclaimed by Croatian owners as part of the reintegration of Eastern Slavonia.

Croatia's nationalist authorities have been accused by U.N. bodies and Western governments of throwing up obstacles to the repatriation of minority Serbs uprooted by the war that erupted over Zagreb's secession from Yugoslavia in 1991.
Critics say Zagreb has blocked returns with red tape and tolerated violent crime against the few Serbs who clung to their homes in reconquered regions, to discourage other Serbs from returning.
The Croatian government concedes not enough was done to deter violence against Serbs, but denies obstructing the return.
The government says almost 15,000 of more than 150,000 Serbs who fled the Krajina enclave in 1995 have returned to Croatia.
However, many thousands of Croat refugees from Bosnia's war have occupied housing in the Krajina region vacated by Serbs, complicating any return of the original residents.
